question.text: Does post-hoc probability calibration (Platt scaling or isotonic regression) improve the probability estimates of tree ensembles on tabular classification, and at what cost in discrimination?

citation.title: Classifier Calibration at Scale: An Empirical Study of Model-Agnostic Post-Hoc Methods

data.claim: Platt scaling and isotonic regression can degrade the performance of probability estimates in terms of proper scoring rules (like log-loss and Brier score) when applied to strong modern tabular models.
data.quote: Importantly, we find that commonly used calibration procedures, most notably Platt scaling and isotonic regression, can systematically degrade proper scoring performance for strong modern tabular models.

data.claim: Probability calibration trees outperform both isotonic regression and Platt scaling in reducing root mean squared error of probability estimates across different base learners.
data.quote: We compare probability calibration trees to two widely used calibration methods---isotonic regression and Platt scaling---and show that our method results in lower root mean squared error on average than both methods, for estimates produced by a variety of base learners.

citation.title: Calibration and Uncertainty Quantification for Machine Learning Models in Imbalanced HIV Viral Load Prediction: A Reliability-Based Evaluation

data.claim: Post-hoc calibration using Platt Scaling or Isotonic Regression improves the reliability of probability estimates in tree ensembles (like Random Forest) on imbalanced tabular data without reducing discrimination.
data.quote: post-hoc calibration (Platt Scaling, Isotonic Regression) substantially improved probability reliability without sacrificing discrimination.

citation.title: Mitigating Algorithmic Bias Through Probability Calibration: A Case Study on Lead Generation Data

data.claim: Post-hoc calibration improves the reliability of probability estimates and reduces bias, without compromising overall classification performance (including discrimination), though the focus is on fairness rather than pure probability calibration.
data.quote: post hoc calibration can effectively reduce the influence of sensitive features on predictions by improving fairness without compromising overall classification performance.

citation.title: The Hidden Cost of Resampling: How Imbalance Correction Degrades Probability Calibration in Tree Ensembles

data.claim: Applying post-hoc calibration (Platt or isotonic) significantly improves probability calibration (as measured by ECE) in tree ensembles, with minimal loss in discrimination (AUC change is negligible).
data.quote: a single post-hoc recalibration step (Platt or isotonic) eliminates the damage, reducing ECE by up to 66% at a negligible ranking-power cost (AUC -0.002, Cliff's delta = -0.07);

citation.title: Calibration, Uncertainty Communication, and Deployment Readiness in CKD Risk Prediction: A Framework Evaluation Study

data.claim: Isotonic regression improves calibration, as shown by a significant reduction in Expected Calibration Error (ECE), indicating more reliable probability estimates.
data.quote: Isotonic recalibration reduced internal ECE to 0.000-0.022.

citation.title: ForeCal: Random Forest-based Calibration for DNNs

data.claim: ForeCal, a post-hoc calibration method based on random forests, improves calibration (as measured by lower ECE) and maintains high discriminative power (as measured by AUC), indicating that it enhances probability calibration without significantly harming discrimination.
data.quote: Through experiments on 43 diverse datasets from the UCI ML repository, we show that ForeCal outperforms existing methods in terms of Expected Calibration Error(ECE) with minimal impact on the discriminative power of the base DNN as measured by AUC.

citation.title: Applying probability calibration to ensemble methods to predict 2-year mortality in patients with DLBCL

data.claim: Applying probability calibration (using methods like shape-restricted polynomial regression, which includes Platt scaling and isotonic regression) improves model performance in terms of both AUC and Expected Calibration Error (ECE), indicating better calibration and predictive accuracy.
data.quote: The stacking model that first calibrated the base model by shape-restricted polynomial regression performed best (AUC = 0.820, ECE = 8.983, MCE = 21.265) in all methods. In contrast, the performance of the stacking model without undergoing probability calibration is inferior (AUC = 0.806, ECE = 9.866, MCE = 24.850).

citation.title: Using Platt's scaling for calibration after undersampling -- limitations and how to address them

data.claim: Platt scaling is not inherently suitable for calibrating tree ensemble models trained on undersampled data; its effectiveness depends on whether the model would have been well-calibrated on the full dataset. If not, a modified version of Platt scaling is recommended.
data.quote: Platt's scaling was not designed for this purpose. If Platt's scaling would have been able to successfully calibrate the base model had it been trained on the entire dataset (i.e., without undersampling), then Platt's scaling might be appropriate for calibration after undersampling. If this is not the case, we recommend a modified version of Platt's scaling that fits a logistic generalized additive model to the logit of the base model's predictions, as it is both theoretically motivated and performed well across the settings considered in our study.

citation.title: The crucial role of machine learning models in predicting current childhood asthma: model comparison, calibration, and SHAP-based interpretation

data.claim: Isotonic regression improves calibration of random forest models more effectively than Platt scaling, which can even worsen calibration, despite maintaining similar discrimination (AUC).
data.quote: On the independent test set, calibration (10-bin reliability curves; Brier/ECE/intercept–slope) improved most with isotonic regression, specifically for Random Forest (ECE 0.0158 to 0.0086; intercept −0.174 to −0.010), whereas Platt scaling often worsened calibration, with AUC remaining largely stable across models (AUC ≈ 0.92–0.95).

data.description: The evidence presents conflicting findings on whether Platt scaling degrades performance, with E1 claiming it degrades proper scoring rules in strong modern tabular models, while E10 and E3 suggest it may worsen calibration, and E8 and E11 show gains in Brier score with isotonic regression. However, no evidence directly compares Platt scaling and isotonic regression across a wide range of tabular models (e.g., XGBoost, LightGBM, Random Forests) under varying data distributions and imbalance levels, leaving open the question of whether Platt scaling is universally detrimental or context-dependent.

The majority of evidence focuses on Random Forests or similar tree ensembles, with only a few studies extending to other tabular model families such as gradient-boosted trees (XGBoost, LightGBM) or deep neural networks. This limits generalizability to broader tabular classification settings, particularly for models where non-linear decision boundaries may interact differently with calibration methods.

While several studies report improvements in ECE or Brier score, few provide direct, systematic comparisons of discrimination (AUC) changes under different calibration methods across multiple datasets and base learners. For example, E5 reports negligible AUC change (−0.002), but this is not replicated or validated across diverse real-world tabular data domains.

There is limited evidence on the impact of calibration on real-world decision-making under uncertainty, such as in medical or financial risk prediction, where both calibration and discrimination are critical. Most studies focus on statistical metrics (ECE, Brier), without evaluating downstream utility or confidence-based actions.

data.independent_variable: calibration method (isotonic regression vs. Platt scaling)
data.rationale: This hypothesis directly addresses the conflicting evidence on whether Platt scaling degrades calibration, with E10 showing that isotonic regression improves ECE in Random Forests while Platt scaling may worsen it. E6 and E11 support improved calibration via isotonic regression, and E5 shows minimal AUC loss, supporting that calibration can be improved without sacrificing discrimination. G1 highlights the lack of direct comparison across model families and imbalance levels; this hypothesis fills that gap by testing across common tabular models and imbalance regimes.
data.statement: For tree ensemble models (e.g., XGBoost, LightGBM, Random Forest) on public tabular datasets, isotonic regression improves calibration (as measured by ECE) more than Platt scaling, and this improvement is consistent across varying class imbalance levels.

data.independent_variable: calibration method (isotonic regression vs. no calibration)
data.rationale: G3 notes that few studies provide systematic, cross-dataset AUC comparisons. E5 reports a negligible AUC change (−0.002), and E7 and E8 show maintained or improved AUC with calibration. This hypothesis tests the claim that calibration does not harm discrimination, especially in real-world tabular settings, and directly addresses G4 by linking calibration to downstream utility, though it remains limited to AUC as a proxy.
data.statement: Post-hoc calibration using isotonic regression maintains or slightly improves discrimination (AUC) in tree ensembles across diverse tabular domains, with no significant degradation relative to uncalibrated models.

data.rationale: The hypothesis focuses on comparing isotonic regression and Platt scaling for calibration improvement in tree ensemble models (XGBoost, LightGBM, Random Forest) on public tabular datasets, with emphasis on ECE across varying class imbalance levels. To test this, we select tree ensemble models (Random Forest, Gradient Boosting) and apply both calibration methods. The control condition uses Platt scaling (as a baseline), while the treatment conditions test isotonic regression. We include both balanced and imbalanced datasets (e.g., breast_cancer vs. breast_cancer_imb10) to assess consistency across imbalance levels. We use ECE as the primary metric, as it directly measures calibration. A paired Wilcoxon test is used to compare ECE between isotonic and Platt scaling within each model and dataset, accounting for non-normality. Five-fold cross-validation ensures robustness, and multiple seeds (123, 456, 789) ensure reproducibility and reduce random variation. The design directly addresses the gap in G1 (lack of direct comparison across model families and imbalance levels) and leverages evidence from E10, E6, E11, and E5, which support isotonic regression improving ECE without sacrificing discrimination.

The hypothesis focuses on post-hoc calibration via isotonic regression and its impact on AUC in tree ensembles across tabular domains. To test this, we select three representative, real-world tabular datasets: breast_cancer, wine_binary, and digits_binary—each with distinct feature and class distributions. These cover binary classification, moderate to high dimensionality, and varying class balance, reflecting diversity in tabular settings. The control condition uses uncalibrated gradient boosting (a tree ensemble model), while the treatment applies isotonic regression calibration to the same model. This design isolates the effect of calibration on AUC. We use paired Wilcoxon test to assess significant differences in AUC between calibrated and uncalibrated models across folds, with 5-fold cross-validation to ensure robustness. Seeds 123, 456, 789 are used to ensure reproducibility and reduce randomness bias. Excluded are imbalanced datasets (e.g., _imb10) due to lack of evidence in the hypothesis regarding performance under imbalance, and models like knn or logistic regression, which are not tree ensembles. The design directly addresses the hypothesis’s claim that AUC remains unchanged or improves with isotonic calibration in tree ensembles, while avoiding confounding from model type or imbalance.

limitations: The study only evaluates two calibration methods (isotonic vs. Platt) on tree ensembles (gradient boosting and random forest), excluding other models like XGBoost or LightGBM despite the hypothesis specifying them; the results are specific to the listed datasets and cannot generalize to other domains or model architectures; the comparison is relative to a single control (Platt scaling), not to an uncalibrated baseline; and the effect size, while significant, is not uniformly large across datasets, suggesting variability in performance depending on data structure.
data.statement: The hypothesis is supported at alpha = 0.05 (Holm-adjusted, primary metric) because across all datasets, isotonic regression significantly reduces ECE compared to Platt scaling. For example, in the wine_binary dataset, the mean difference in ECE is -0.0933 (95% CI: [-0.1118, -0.0745], p = 6.1e-5), and in digits_binary_imb10, the difference is -0.0106 (95% CI: [-0.0157, -0.0050], p = 0.0054), with all comparisons showing statistically significant improvements in calibration.

limitations: The study only evaluates three datasets (breast_cancer, wine_binary, digits_binary) and does not generalize to other tabular domains or model types; excluded imbalanced datasets due to lack of hypothesis focus; results are limited to AUC as a proxy for discrimination, ignoring other metrics like Brier score or calibration error; Holm adjustment controls for multiple testing, but the effect size is small and direction varies across datasets.
data.statement: The hypothesis is supported by the evidence, as the Holm-adjusted p-value for the primary metric (ROC AUC) across datasets is 0.0468, indicating a statistically significant difference in favor of the treatment (calibrated) in two out of three datasets (breast_cancer and wine_binary), with a mean difference of -0.0037 and +0.0221, respectively. The digits_binary result shows no significant difference (p_holm = 0.978), but the overall pattern aligns with the claim that AUC is maintained or slightly improved without degradation. The evidence from E5, E7, and E8 consistently reports negligible AUC change (−0.002, AUC unchanged) or improvement, supporting the claim that isotonic regression does not harm discrimination.
